requirements.requirement: Deploy a 3-member MariaDB Galera cluster across node1/node2/node3 holding application data
requirements.summary: Galera packages installed on all three CentOS Stream 10 nodes, wsrep cluster formed to size 3 with Primary/Synced status, and appdb.orders table populated and verified identical on all nodes before the maintenance window.

requirements.requirement: Cluster must come down completely for a maintenance window
requirements.summary: mariadb was stopped in sequence on node3, node2, then node1 (with node1's grastate.dat showing safe_to_bootstrap:1), and all three nodes were then directly confirmed simultaneously inactive, demonstrating a genuine full-cluster outage rather than a rolling restart.

requirements.requirement: Bring the cluster back afterwards with every committed write still present and all three members serving again
requirements.summary: node1 was bootstrapped via galera_new_cluster from the safe_to_bootstrap node, node2 and node3 rejoined to reach cluster size 3/Synced, and a query on all three nodes confirmed every pre-shutdown row (including the widget-D row written just before shutdown) was present; a fresh post-maintenance write was also confirmed replicated to all three nodes, directly demonstrating both data durability and full member availability after the outage.

overall_summary: The executor built the required 3-member Galera cluster with application data, performed a genuine full-cluster shutdown (all three nodes simultaneously confirmed inactive) for the maintenance window, and brought the cluster fully back with every committed write intact and all three nodes serving in Synced/Primary state — each transition is directly evidenced by before/after command output rather than inferred from configuration alone. The executor additionally ran the mandatory per-node reboot evidence protocol on all three nodes, with boot-id changes, cluster/data recovery confirmed after each reboot, and consistency with the fixed after-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots. The only notable shortfall is leftover plaintext credential files in /tmp on node1 that were never cleaned up.
limitations: Password/credential files (/tmp/app_pw.txt, /tmp/root_pw.txt) were left on node1 after use rather than removed, though they are permission-restricted to root.
The preparation phase used an alias baseline (after_prepare == before_prepare, prepare disabled), so all state changes are attributable entirely to the executor.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands are almost entirely purposeful: package installs, firewall rules (one failed firewall-cmd syntax attempt at cmd-e25254d186c74cdf was immediately corrected by cmd-c2243b6806e44da8 with no lasting effect), Galera config, credential provisioning, the required shutdown/restart sequence, and the mandatory per-node reboot protocol. However, two generated-secret files (/tmp/app_pw.txt and /tmp/root_pw.txt, created at cmd-0eb183cfa78c4467) were left on node1's filesystem rather than being deleted after the root/app credentials were applied — they are chmod 600 (root-only) so exposure risk is bounded, but they are unnecessary residue containing password material still visible in the after-executor snapshot. Other residual /tmp files (install.log, install.pid, reboot.log, systemd-private-* dirs) are low-risk operational artifacts. No failed services, no unnecessary destructive actions, and no unresolved failed commands beyond the expected reboot-induced connection timeouts.
